cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 95% Student-t confidence half-width for a standard deviation of 1 and a sample of 50
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.284196855. Independently derived from the documented Student-t half-width t_(1-alpha/2, size-1) * standard_dev / sqrt(size): scipy.stats.t.isf(0.05/2, 49) = 2.0095752371292397 on size-1 = 49 degrees of freedom, so 2.0095752371292397 * 1 / sqrt(50) = 0.2841968554957299 -> 0.284196855 at 9 dp. The t multiplier is visibly larger than the normal 1.95996 of CONFIDENCE.NORM, which is what distinguishes the two functions

cases.description: A non-integer sample size, which the documentation says is truncated
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "If size is not an integer, it is truncated", so 50.9 must behave exactly as 50. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine size of 50.9 (49.9 degrees of freedom) would give 0.281545

Excel documents: "If size equals 1, CONFIDENCE.T returns #DIV/0! error value." This is the one place the .T variant's error contract differs from CONFIDENCE.NORM's, which returns #NUM! only below size 1 and computes normally at size 1: with size 1 there are zero degrees of freedom for the t distribution
Excel documents: "If alpha <= 0 or alpha >= 1, CONFIDENCE.T returns the #NUM! error value."
Excel documents: "If standard_dev <= 0, CONFIDENCE.T returns the #NUM! error value."
Excel documents: "If any argument is nonnumeric, CONFIDENCE.T returns the #VALUE! error value."
